subject: Ophthalmology
question: A 65-year-old man with a 16 year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus presents complaining of poor eye sight and blurred vision. Visual acuity measured using a Snellen chart is reduced to 6/12 in the right eye and 6/18 in the left eye. Fundoscopy reveals a number of yellow deposits in the left eye consistent with drusen formation. Similar changes but to a lesser extent are seen in the right eye. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Drusen = Dry macular degeneration

Age related macular degeneration Age related macular degeneration is the most common cause of blindness in the UK. Degeneration of the central retina (macula) is the key feature with changes usually bilateral. Traditionally two forms of macular degeneration are seen: xdry (geographic atrophy) macular degeneration: characterised by drusen - yellow round spots in Bruch's membrane xwet (exudative, neovascular) macular degeneration: characterised by choroidal neovascularisation. Leakage of serous fluid and blood can subsequently result in a rapid loss of vision. Carries worst prognosis Recently there has been a move to a more updated classification: xearly age related macular degeneration (non-exudative, age related maculopathy): drusen and alterations to the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) xlate age related macular degeneration (neovascularisation, exudative) Risk factors xage: most patients are over 60 years of age xsmoking xfamily history xmore common in Caucasians xhigh cumulative sunlight exposure xfemale sex Features xreduced visual acuity: 'blurred', 'distorted' vision, central vision is affected first xcentral scotomas xfundoscopy: drusen, pigmentary changes Investigation and diagnosis xoptical coherence tomography: provide cross sectional views of the macula xif neovascularisation is present fluorescein angiography is performed General management xstop smoking xhigh dose of beta-carotene, vitamins C and E, and zinc may help to slow down visual loss for patients with established macular degeneration. Supplements should be avoided in smokers due to an increased risk of lung cancer Dry macular degeneration - no current medical treatments Wet macular degeneration xphotocoagulation xphotodynamic therapy

xanti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) treatments: intravitreal ranibizumab

subject: Ophthalmology
question: Which one of the following is associated with the Holmes-Adie pupil?

options.D: An increased of developing multiple sclerosis

explanation:
Holmes ADIe = DIlated pupil, females, absent leg reflexes

Holmes-Adie pupil Holmes-Adie pupil is a benign condition most commonly seen in women. It is one of the differentials of a dilated pupil. Overview xunilateral in 80% of cases xdilated pupil xonce the pupil has constricted it remains small for an abnormally long time xslowly reactive to accommodation but very poorly (if at all) to light Holmes-Adie syndrome xassociation of Holmes-Adie pupil with absent ankle/knee reflexes

subject: Ophthalmology
question: A 71-year-old man presents with a burning sensation around his right eye. On examination an erythematous blistering rash can be seen in the right trigeminal distribution. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus Herpes zoster ophthalmicus (HZO) describes the reactivation of the varicella zoster virus in the area supplied by the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve. It accounts for around 10% of case of shingles. Features xvesicular rash around the eye, which may or may not involve the actual eye itself xHutchinson's sign: rash on the tip or side of the nose. Indicates nasociliary involvement and is a strong risk factor for ocular involvement Management xoral antiviral treatment for 7-10 days, ideally started within 72 hours. Topical antiviral treatment is not given in HZO xoral corticosteroids may reduce the duration of pain but do not reduce the incidence of post- herpetic neuralgia xocular involvement requires urgent ophthalmology review Complications xocular: conjunctivitis, keratitis, episcleritis, anterior uveitis xptosis xpost-herpetic neuralgia

subject: Ophthalmology
question: Which one of the following is least associated with the development of optic atrophy?
explanation: Optic atrophy Optic atrophy is seen as pale, well demarcated disc on fundoscopy. It is usually bilateral and causes a gradual loss of vision*. Causes may be acquired or congenital Acquired causes xmultiple sclerosis xpapilloedema (longstanding) xraised intraocular pressure (e.g. glaucoma, tumour) xretinal damage (e.g. choroiditis, retinitis pigmentosa) xischaemia xtoxins: tobacco amblyopia, quinine, methanol, arsenic, lead xnutritional: vitamin B1, B2, B6 and B12 deficiency Congenital causes xFriedreich's ataxia xmitochondrial disorders e.g. Leber's optic atrophy xDIDMOAD - the association of cranial Diabetes Insipidus, Diabetes Mellitus, Optic Atrophy and Deafness (also known as Wolfram's syndrome) *strictly speaking optic atrophy is a descriptive term, it is the optic neuropathy that results in visual loss

subject: Ophthalmology
question: A 34-year-old woman presents complaining of headaches. Examination of her pupils using a light shone alternately in each eye reveals that when the light is shone in the right eye both pupils constrict but when the light source immediately moves to the left eye both eyes appear to dilate. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: This is the 'swinging light test' and reveals a relative afferent pupillary defect. As there is a defect in the afferent nerve on the left side the pupils constrict less than normal, giving the impression of dilation. Given her age, multiple sclerosis causing optic neuritis is the likely underlying diagnosis. Optic neuritis typically causes a dull ache in the region of the eye which is aggravated by movement Relative afferent pupillary defect Also known as the Marcus-Gunn pupil, a relative afferent pupillary defect is found by the 'swinging light test'. It is caused by a lesion anterior to the optic chiasm i.e. optic nerve or retina Causes xretina: detachment xoptic nerve: optic neuritis e.g. multiple sclerosis Pathway of pupillary light reflex xafferent: retina --> optic nerve --> lateral geniculate body --> midbrain xefferent: Edinger-Westphal nucleus (midbrain) --> oculomotor nerve

subject: Ophthalmology
question: A 65-year-old man with a known history of Paget's disease is noted to have irregular dark red lines radiating from the optic nerve. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation: This is a typical description of angioid retinal streaks which are associated with Paget's disease Angioid retinal streaks Angioid retinal streaks are seen on fundoscopy as irregular dark red streaks radiating from the optic nerve head. They are caused by degeneration, calcification and breaks in Bruch's membrane . Causes xpseudoxanthoma elasticum xEhler-Danlos syndrome xPaget's disease xsickle-cell anaemia xacromegaly

question: A 64-year-old woman presents with bilateral sore eyelids. She also complains of her eyes being dry all the time. On examination her eyelid margins are erythematous at the margins but are not swollen. Of the given options, what is the most appropriate initial management?

options.A: Topical chloramphenicol + mechanical removal of lid debris
options.D: Hot compresses + mechanical removal of lid debris

explanation:
Artificial tears may also be given for symptom relief of blepharitis Blepharitis Blepharitis is inflammation of the eyelid margins. It may due to either meibomian gland dysfunction (common, posterior blepharitis) or seborrhoeic dermatitis/staphylococcal infection (less common, anterior blepharitis). Blepharitis is also more common in patients with rosacea The meibomian glands secrete oil on to the eye surface to prevent rapid evaporation of the tear film. Anyproblem affecting the meibomian glands (as in blepharitis) can hence cause drying of the eyes which in turns leads to irritation Features xsymptoms are usually bilateral xgrittiness and discomfort, particularly around the eyelid margins xeyes may be sticky in the morning xeyelid margins may be red. Swollen eyelids may be seen in staphylococcal blepharitis xstyes and chalazions are more common in patients with blepharitis xsecondary conjunctivitis may occur Management xsoftening of the lid margin using hot compresses twice a day xmechanical removal of the debris from lid margins - cotton wool buds dipped in a mixture of cooled boiled water and baby shampoo is often used* xartificial tears may be given for symptom relief in people with dry eyes or an abnormal tear film

*an alternative is sodium bicarbonate, a teaspoonful in a cup of cooled water that has recently been boiled

subject: Ophthalmology
question: A 34-year-old man is referred to ophthalmology following a deterioration in his vision. He is noted to be tall with thin, long fingers and a degree of learning disabilities. Following review he is suspected as having a displacement of his lens on the right side. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation: The presence of learning difficulties points to a diagnosis of homocystinuria rather than Marfan's syndrome. Homocystinuria Homocystinuria is a rare autosomal recessive disease caused by deficiency of cystathionine beta synthase. This results in an accumulation of homocysteine which is then oxidized to homocystine. Features xoften patients have fine, fair hair xmusculoskeletal: may be similar to Marfan's - arachnodactyly etc xneurological patients may have learning difficulties, seizures xocular: downwards (inferonasal) dislocation of lens xincreased risk of arterial and venous thromboembolism xalso malar flush, livedo reticularis Diagnosis is made by the cyanide-nitroprusside test, which is also positive in cystinuria Treatment is vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) supplements

subject: Ophthalmology
question: A 62-year-old man presents with sudden visual loss in his right eye. He is otherwise asymptomatic. Which one of the following conditions is least likely to be responsible?

options.B: Occlusion of the central retinal vein
options.C: Occlusion of the central retinal artery

explanation:
Whilst optic neuritis can present with sudden loss, in this 62-year-old man it is the least likely option. Typically there is a unilateral decrease in visual acuity over hours or days. There may be poor discrimination of colours and eye pain on movement Sudden painless loss of vision The most common causes of a sudden painless loss of vision are as follows: xischaemic optic neuropathy (e.g. temporal arteritis or atherosclerosis) xocclusion of central retinal vein xocclusion of central retinal artery xvitreous haemorrhage xretinal detachment Ischaemic optic neuropathy xmay be due to arteritis (e.g. temporal arteritis) or atherosclerosis (e.g. hypertensive, diabetic older patient) xdue to occlusion of the short posterior ciliary arteries, causing damage to the optic nerve xaltitudinal field defects are seen Central retinal vein occlusion xincidence increases with age, more common than arterial occlusion xcauses: glaucoma, polycythaemia, hypertension xsevere retinal haemorrhages are usually seen on fundoscopy

Central retinal artery occlusion xdue to thromboembolism (from atherosclerosis) or arteritis (e.g. temporal arteritis) xfeatures include afferent pupillary defect, 'cherry red' spot on a pale retina Vitreous haemorrhage xcauses: diabetes, bleeding disorders xfeatures may include sudden visual loss, dark spots Retinal detachment xfeatures of vitreous detachment, which may precede retinal detachment, include flashes of light or floaters (see below) Differentiating posterior vitreous detachment, retinal detachment and vitreous haemorrhage

Posterior vitreous detachment Retinal detachment Vitreous haemorrhage

Flashes of light (photopsia) - in the peripheral field of vision Floaters, often on the temporal side of the central vision Dense shadow that starts peripherally progresses towards the central vision A veil or curtain over the field of vision Straight lines appear curved Central visual loss Large bleeds cause sudden visual loss Moderate bleeds may be described as numerous dark spots Small bleeds may cause floaters

subject: Ophthalmology
question: A 63-year-old man presents to his GP complaining of pain in his right eye. On examination the sclera is red and the pupil is dilated with a hazy cornea. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Red eye - glaucoma or uveitis? xglaucoma: severe pain, haloes, 'semi-dilated' pupil xuveitis: small, fixed oval pupil, ciliary flush

Red eye There are many possible causes of a red eye. It is important to be able to recognise the causes which require urgent referral to an ophthalmologist. Below is a brief summary of the key distinguishing features Acute angle closure glaucoma xsevere pain (may be ocular or headache) xdecreased visual acuity, patient sees haloes xsemi-dilated pupil xhazy cornea Anterior uveitis xacute onset xpain xblurred vision and photophobia xsmall, fixed oval pupil, ciliary flush Scleritis xsevere pain (may be worse on movement) and tenderness xmay be underlying autoimmune disease e.g. rheumatoid arthritis Conjunctivitis xpurulent discharge if bacterial, clear discharge if viral Subconjunctival haemorrhage

xhistory of trauma or coughing bouts

subject: Ophthalmology
question: A 74-year-old man presents to ophthalmology clinic after seeing his optician. They have noticed raised intraocular pressure and decreased peripheral vision. His past medical history includes asthma and type 2 diabetes mellitus. What is the most appropriate treatment given the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
A prostaglandin analogue should be used first-line in patients with a history of asthma. Primary open-angle glaucoma: management The majority of patients with primary open-angle glaucoma are managed with eye drops. These aim to lower intra-ocular pressure which in turn has been shown to prevent progressive loss of visual field.

Medication Mode of action Notes

Prostaglandin analogues (e.g. Latanoprost) Increases uveoscleral outflow Once daily administration Adverse effects include brown pigmentation of the iris Beta-blockers (e.g. Timolol) Reduces aqueous production Should be avoided in asthmatics and patients with heart block Sympathomimetics (e.g. Brimonidine, an alpha2- adrenoceptor agonist) Reduces aqueous production and increases outflow Avoid if taking MAOI or tricyclic antidepressants Adverse effects include hyperaemia Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (e.g. Dorzolamide) Reduces aqueous production Systemic absorption may cause sulphonamide-like reactions Miotics (e.g. Pilocarpine) Increases uveoscleral outflow Adverse effects included a constricted pupil, headache and blurred vision

Surgery in the form of a trabeculectomy may be considered in refractory cases.

subject: Ophthalmology
question: A 54-year-old woman presents with a persistent watery left eye for the past 4 days. On examination there is erythema and swelling of the inner canthus of the left eye. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Lacrimal duct problems

Dacryocystitis is infection of the lacrimal sac Features xwatering eye (epiphora) xswelling and erythema at the inner canthus of the eye Management is with systemic antibiotics. Intravenous antibiotics are indicated if there is associated periorbital cellulitis

Congenital lacrimal duct obstruction affects around 5-10% of newborns. It is bilateral in around 20% of cases Features xwatering eye (even if not crying) xsecondary infection may occur Symptoms resolve in 99% of cases by 12 months of age

subject: Ophthalmology
question: A 71-year-old man presents with severe pain around his right eye and vomiting. On examination the right eye is red and decreased visual acuity is noted. Which one of the following options is the most appropriate initial treatment?
explanation:
Treatment of acute glaucoma - acetazolamide + pilocarpine

Acute angle closure glaucoma Glaucoma is a group disorders characterised by optic neuropathy due, in the majority of patients, to raised intraocular pressure (IOP). It is now recognised that a minority of patients with raised IOP do not have glaucoma and vice versa

In acute angle closure glaucoma (AACG) there is a rise in IOP secondary to an impairment of aqueous outflow. Factors predisposing to AACG include: xhypermetropia (long-sightedness) xpupillary dilatation xlens growth associated with age Features xsevere pain: may be ocular or headache xdecreased visual acuity xsymptoms worse with mydriasis (e.g. watching TV in a dark room) xhard, red eye xhaloes around lights xsemi-dilated non-reacting pupil xcorneal oedema results in dull or hazy cornea xsystemic upset may be seen, such as nausea and vomiting and even abdominal pain Management xurgent referral to an ophthalmologist xmanagement options include reducing aqueous secretions with acetazolamide and inducing papillary constriction with topical pilocarpine

question: A 35-year-old man presents with visual problems. He has had very poor vision in the dark for a long time but is now worried as he is developing 'tunnel vision'. He states his grandfather had a similar problem and was registered blind in his 50's. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Retinitis pigmentosa - night blindness + funnel vision

Retinitis pigmentosa Retinitis pigmentosa primarily affects the peripheral retina resulting in funnel vision Features xnight blindness is often the initial sign xfunnel vision (the preferred term for tunnel vision) xfundoscopy: black bone spicule-shaped pigmentation in the peripheral retina, mottling of the retinal pigment epithelium Associated diseases xRefsum disease: cerebellar ataxia, peripheral neuropathy, deafness, ichthyosis xUsher syndrome xabetalipoproteinemia xLawrence-Moon-Biedl syndrome xKearns-Sayre syndrome xAlport's syndrome

question: A 60-year-old woman who has recently started treatment for polymyalgia rheumatica presents with a five day history of headaches and reduced vision on the right side since this morning There is no eye pain but the there is a 'large, dark shadow' covering the superior visual field on the right side. On examination she has a tender, palpable right temporal artery. What is the most likely explanation for the reduced vision?
explanation: Temporal arteritis Temporal arteritis is large vessel vasculitis which overlaps with polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR). Histology shows changes which characteristically 'skips' certain sections of affected artery whilst damaging others. Features xtypically patient > 60 years old xusually rapid onset (e.g. < 1 month) xheadache (found in 85%) xjaw claudication (65%) xvisual disturbances secondary to anterior ischemic optic neuropathy xtender, palpable temporal artery xfeatures of PMR: aching, morning stiffness in proximal limb muscles (not weakness) xalso lethargy, depression, low-grade fever, anorexia, night sweats Investigations xraised inflammatory markers: ESR > 50 mm/hr (note ESR < 30 in 10% of patients). CRP may also be elevated xtemporal artery biopsy: skip lesions may be present xnote creatine kinase and EMG normal Treatment xhigh-dose prednisolone - there should be a dramatic response, if not the diagnosis should be reconsidered xurgent ophthalmology review. Patients with visual symptoms should be seen the same-day by an ophthalmologist. Visual damage is often irreversible

question: Each one of the following is a cause of a mydriatic pupil, except:
explanation:

question: A 45-year-old woman with Graves' disease comes for review. She has recently been diagnosed with thyroid eye disease and is being considered for radiotherapy. Over the past three days her right eye has become red and painful. On examination there is proptosis and erythema of the right eye. Visual acuity is 6/9 in both eyes. What complication is she most likely to have developed?
explanation:
Thyroid eye disease Thyroid eye disease affects between 25-50% of patients with Graves' disease. It is thought to be caused by an autoimmune response against an autoantigen, possibly the TSH receptor, which in turns causes retro-orbital inflammation. The patient may be eu-, hypo- or hyperthyroid at the time of presentation

Prevention xsmoking is the most important modifiable risk factor for the development of thyroid eye disease xradioiodine treatment may increase the inflammatory symptoms seen in thyroid eye disease. In a recent study of patients with Graves' disease around 15% developed, or had worsening of, eye disease.

Prednisolone may help reduce the risk

Features xexophthalmos xconjunctival oedema xoptic disc swelling xophthalmoplegia xinability to close the eye lids may lead to sore, dry eyes. If severe and untreated patients can be at risk of exposure keratopathy

Management xtopical lubricants may be needed to help prevent corneal inflammation caused by exposure xsteroids xradiotherapy xsurgery

question: Which one of the following is not a risk factor for primary open-angle glaucoma?
explanation:

Primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG, also referred to as chronic simple glaucoma) is present in around 2% of people older than 40 years. Other than age, risk factors include: xfamily history xblack patients xmyopia xhypertension xdiabetes mellitus

question: A 70-year-old man is investigated for blurred vision. Fundoscopy reveals drusen, retinal epithelial and macular neovascularisation. A diagnosis of age related macular degeneration is suspected. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
explanation:
Age related macular degeneration Age related macular degeneration is the most common cause of blindness in the UK. Degeneration of the central retina (macula) is the key feature with changes usually bilateral.

Traditionally two forms of macular degeneration are seen: xdry (geographic atrophy) macular degeneration: characterised by drusen - yellow round spots in Bruch's membrane xwet (exudative, neovascular) macular degeneration: characterised by choroidal neovascularisation.

Leakage of serous fluid and blood can subsequently result in a rapid loss of vision. Carries worst prognosis

Recently there has been a move to a more updated classification: xearly age related macular degeneration (non-exudative, age related maculopathy): drusen and alterations to the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) xlate age related macular degeneration (neovascularisation, exudative) Risk factors xage: most patients are over 60 years of age xsmoking xfamily history xmore common in Caucasians xhigh cumulative sunlight exposure xfemale sex

Features xreduced visual acuity: 'blurred', 'distorted' vision, central vision is affected first xcentral scotomas xfundoscopy: drusen, pigmentary changes

Investigation and diagnosis xoptical coherence tomography: provide cross sectional views of the macula xif neovascularisation is present fluorescein angiography is performed General management xstop smoking xhigh dose of beta-carotene, vitamins C and E, and zinc may help to slow down visual loss for patients with established macular degeneration. Supplements should be avoided in smokers due to an increased risk of lung cancer

explanation:
Sudden painless loss of vision

patient) xdue to occlusion of the short posterior ciliary arteries, causing damage to the optic nerve xaltitudinal field defects are seen

question: A 70-year-old woman presents with loss of vision in her left eye. For the past two weeks she has painful frontal headaches and has been feeling generally lethargic. On examination visual acuity is 6/9 in the right eye but on the left side only hand movements can be made seen. Fundoscopy of the left side reveals a pale and oedematous optic disc. What is the most likely diagnosis?.
explanation:
This patient has likely developed anterior ischemic optic neuropathy on the left side Temporal arteritis

Temporal arteritis is large vessel vasculitis which overlaps with polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR). Histology shows changes which characteristically 'skips' certain sections of affected artery whilst damaging others.

Features xtypically patient > 60 years old xusually rapid onset (e.g. < 1 month) xheadache (found in 85%) xjaw claudication (65%) xvisual disturbances secondary to anterior ischemic optic neuropathy xtender, palpable temporal artery xfeatures of PMR: aching, morning stiffness in proximal limb muscles (not weakness) xalso lethargy, depression, low-grade fever, anorexia, night sweats Investigations xraised inflammatory markers: ESR > 50 mm/hr (note ESR < 30 in 10% of patients). subject: Ophthalmology
question: A 52-year-old old man who has a history of alcohol excess is brought to the Emergency Department by paramedics. He is a frequent attender and this time has a laceration on his scalp following a fall. Whilst examining him he seems confused and complains of problems with his vision. Which one of the following is the most commonly found ocular abnormality in patients with Wernicke's encephalopathy?
explanation:
Wernicke's encephalopathy

Wernicke's encephalopathy is a neuropsychiatric disorder caused by thiamine deficiency which is most commonly seen in alcoholics. Rarer causes include: persistent vomiting, stomach cancer, dietary deficiency. A classic triad of nystagmus, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia may occur. In Wernicke's encephalopathy petechial haemorrhages occur in a variety of structures in the brain including the mamillary bodies and ventricle walls Features xnystagmus (the most common ocular sign) xophthalmoplegia xataxia xconfusion, altered GCS xperipheral sensory neuropathy Investigations xdecreased red cell transketolase xMRI Treatment is with urgent replacement of thiamine

subject: Ophthalmology
question: Which one of the following is not a feature of background diabetic retinopathy?

options.D: Seen in both type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus

explanation:
Cotton wool spots are seen in pre-proliferative retinopathy Diabetic retinopathy Diabetic retinopathy is the most common cause of blindness in adults aged 35-65 years-old. Hyperglycaemia is thought to cause increased retinal blood flow and abnormal metabolism in the retinal vessel walls. This precipitates damage to endothelial cells and pericytes

Endothelial dysfunction leads to increased vascular permeability which causes the characteristic exudates seen on fundoscopy. Pericyte dysfunction predisposes to the formation of microaneurysms. Neovasculization is thought to be caused by the production of growth factors in response to retinal ischaemia

In exams you are most likely to be asked about the characteristic features of the various stages/types of diabetic retinopathy. Recently a new classification system has been proposed, dividing patients into those with nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR) and those with proliferative retinopathy (PDR):

Traditional classification New classification Background retinopathy xmicroaneurysms (dots) xblot haemorrhages (<=3) xhard exudates Pre-proliferative retinopathy xcotton wool spots (soft exudates; ischaemic nerve fibres) x> 3 blot haemorrhages xvenous beading/looping xdeep/dark cluster haemorrhages xmore common in Type I DM, treat with laser photocoagulation Mild NPDR x1 or more microaneurysm Moderate NPDR xmicroaneurysms xblot haemorrhages xhard exudates xcotton wool spots, venous beading/looping and intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMA) less severe than in severe NPDR Severe NPDR xblot haemorrhages and microaneurysms in 4 quadrants xvenous beading in at least 2 quadrants xIRMA in at least 1 quadrant

Proliferative retinopathy xretinal neovascularisation - may lead to vitrous haemorrhage xfibrous tissue forming anterior to retinal disc xmore common in Type I DM, 50% blind in 5 years Maculopathy xbased on location rather than severity, anything is potentially serious xhard exudates and other 'background' changes on macula xcheck visual acuity xmore common in Type II DM

question: A 65-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with visual problems. She has rheumatoid arthritis, depression and takes medication to control her blood pressure. Over the past few days she has been getting troublesome headaches and blurred vision but today has noted a marked reduction in vision in the right eye. On examination her right eye is red, has a sluggish pupil and a corrected visual acuity 6/30. Her medication has recently been changed. Which one of the following drugs is most likely to have precipitated this event?
explanation:
Drugs which may precipitate acute glaucoma include anticholinergics and tricyclic antidepressants Acute angle closure glaucoma Glaucoma is a group disorders characterised by optic neuropathy due, in the majority of patients, to raised intraocular pressure (IOP). It is now recognised that a minority of patients with raised IOP do not have glaucoma and vice versa

In acute angle closure glaucoma (AACG) there is a rise in IOP secondary to an impairment of aqueous outflow.

Factors predisposing to AACG include: xhypermetropia (long-sightedness) xpupillary dilatation xlens growth associated with age

Features xsevere pain: may be ocular or headache xdecreased visual acuity xsymptoms worse with mydriasis (e.g. watching TV in a dark room) xhard, red eye xhaloes around lights xsemi-dilated non-reacting pupil xcorneal oedema results in dull or hazy cornea xsystemic upset may be seen, such as nausea and vomiting and even abdominal pain

question: A 72-year-old woman presents with a vesicular rash around her left eye. The left eye is red and there is a degree of photophobia. A presumptive diagnosis of herpes zoster ophthalmicus is made and an urgent referral to ophthalmology is made. What treatment is she most likely to be given?
explanation:
Herpes zoster ophthalmicus Herpes zoster ophthalmicus (HZO) describes the reactivation of the varicella zoster virus in the area supplied by the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve. It accounts for around 10% of case of shingles.

question: Which one of the following features is not characteristic of optic neuritis?

question: A 74-year-old man presents with a severe throbbing headache on the right side of his head. He has now had this pain for around 6-7 days but reports no obvious trigger. There have been no visual disturbances or episodes of limb weakness. Neurological examination is unremarkable. The right side of his head is tender to touch but he cannot remember falling. Given the likely diagnosis what is the most important initial step?

options.B: Arrange an urgent orbital x-ray for suspected blow-out fracture
options.C: Arrange an urgent temporal artery biopsy

explanation:
This patient has temporal arteritis and requires high-dose oral steroids to prevent ocular complications

Temporal arteritis Temporal arteritis is large vessel vasculitis which overlaps with polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR). Histology shows changes which characteristically 'skips' certain sections of affected artery whilst damaging others.

Features xtypically patient > 60 years old xusually rapid onset (e.g. < 1 month) xheadache (found in 85%) xjaw claudication (65%) xvisual disturbances secondary to anterior ischemic optic neuropathy xtender, palpable temporal artery xfeatures of PMR: aching, morning stiffness in proximal limb muscles (not weakness) xalso lethargy, depression, low-grade fever, anorexia, night sweats

question: A 47-year-old female with a history of rheumatoid arthritis presents with a painful and red left eye. Visual acuity is normal. Fundoscopy is also unremarkable. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Scleritis is painful, episcleritis is not painful

A key way to discriminate between scleritis and episcleritis is the presence of pain. Keratoconjunctivitis sicca is usually bilateral and associated more with dryness, burning and itch Rheumatoid arthritis: ocular manifestations Ocular manifestations of rheumatoid arthritis are common, with 25% of patients having eye problems

Ocular manifestations xkeratoconjunctivitis sicca (most common) xepiscleritis (erythema) xscleritis (erythema and pain) xcorneal ulceration xkeratitis

Iatrogenic xsteroid-induced cataracts xchloroquine retinopathy

subject: Ophthalmology
question: A 43-year-old who is noted to have a high-arched palate, arachnodactyly and a late-systolic murmur presents with visual problems. Which one of the following eye disorders is most associated with his underlying condition?
explanation:
This patient has features consistent with Marfan's syndrome. Whilst glaucoma and retinal detachment are seen they are not as common as superotemporal ectopia lentis (upwards lens dislocation), which is seen in around 50% of patients. Inferonasal ectopia lentis is characteristic of homocystinuria

Mitral valve prolapse may cause a late-systolic murmur. This feature helps distinguish the above description from that of a patient with homocystinuria Marfan's syndrome Marfan's syndrome is an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder. It is caused by a defect in the fibrillin-1 gene on chromosome 15 and affects around 1 in 3,000 people. Features xtall stature with arm span to height ratio > 1.05 xhigh-arched palate xarachnodactyly xpectus excavatum xpes planus xscoliosis of > 20 degrees xheart: dilation of the aortic sinuses (seen in 90%) which may lead to aortic aneurysm, aortic dissection, aortic regurgitation, mitral valve prolapse (75%), xlungs: repeated pneumothoraces xeyes: upwards lens dislocation (superotemporal ectopia lentis), blue sclera, myopia xdural ectasia (ballooning of the dural sac at the lumbosacral level)

The life expectancy of patients used to be around 40-50 years. With the advent of regular echocardiography monitoring and beta-blocker/ACE-inhibitor therapy this has improved significantly over recent years. Aortic dissection and other cardiovascular problems remain the leading cause of death however.

subject: Ophthalmology
question: A 40-year-old man presents with bilateral dry, gritty eyes. A diagnosis of blepharitis is considered. Which one of the following is least likely to be associated with blepharitis?
explanation:
Blepharitis Blepharitis is inflammation of the eyelid margins. It may due to either meibomian gland dysfunction (common, posterior blepharitis) or seborrhoeic dermatitis/staphylococcal infection (less common, anterior blepharitis). Blepharitis is also more common in patients with rosacea The meibomian glands secrete oil on to the eye surface to prevent rapid evaporation of the tear film.

Any problem affecting the meibomian glands (as in blepharitis) can hence cause drying of the eyes which in turns leads to irritation Features xsymptoms are usually bilateral xgrittiness and discomfort, particularly around the eyelid margins xeyes may be sticky in the morning xeyelid margins may be red. Swollen eyelids may be seen in staphylococcal blepharitis xstyes and chalazions are more common in patients with blepharitis xsecondary conjunctivitis may occur

Management xsoftening of the lid margin using hot compresses twice a day xmechanical removal of the debris from lid margins - cotton wool buds dipped in a mixture of cooled boiled water and baby shampoo is often used* xartificial tears may be given for symptom relief in people with dry eyes or an abnormal tear film *an alternative is sodium bicarbonate, a teaspoonful in a cup of cooled water that has recently been boiled

subject: Ophthalmology
question: Which one of the following best describes the action of latanoprost in the management of primary open-angle glaucoma?
explanation:
Primary open-angle glaucoma: management The majority of patients with primary open-angle glaucoma are managed with eye drops. These aim to lower intra-ocular pressure which in turn has been shown to prevent progressive loss of visual field.

Medication Mode of action Notes

Prostaglandin analogues (e.g. Latanoprost) Increases uveoscleral outflow Once daily administration Adverse effects include brown pigmentation of the iris Beta-blockers (e.g. Timolol) Reduces aqueous production Should be avoided in asthmatics and patients with heart block Sympathomimetics (e.g. Brimonidine, an alpha2- adrenoceptor agonist) Reduces aqueous production and increases outflow Avoid if taking MAOI or tricyclic antidepressants Adverse effects include hyperaemia Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (e.g. Dorzolamide) Reduces aqueous production Systemic absorption may cause sulphonamide-like reactions Miotics (e.g. Pilocarpine) Increases uveoscleral outflow Adverse effects included a constricted pupil, headache and blurred vision

Surgery in the form of a trabeculectomy may be considered in refractory cases.

question: A 25-year-old woman presents with a one-day history of a painful and red left eye. She describes how her eye is continually streaming tears. On examination she exhibits a degree of photophobia in the affected eye and application of fluorescein demonstrates a dendritic pattern of staining. Visual acuity is 6/6 in both eyes. What is the most appropriate management?
explanation:
This patient has a dendritic corneal ulcer. Topical aciclovir and ophthalmology review is required. Giving a topical steroid in this situation could be disastrous as it may worsen the infection.

Herpes simplex keratitis Herpes simplex keratitis most commonly presents with a dendritic corneal ulcer

Features xred, painful eye xphotophobia xepiphora xvisual acuity may be decreased xfluorescein staining may show an epithelial ulcer

Management ximmediate referral to an ophthalmologist xtopical aciclovir

question: A 24-year-old man who has a family history of retinitis pigmentosa is reviewed in the ophthalmology clinic. He reports worsening vision over the past few months. During fundoscopy, which of the following findings with most support a diagnosis of retinitis pigmentosa?

options.A: Pigmented scrambled egg appearance concentrated around the macula
options.B: Central irregular pigmentation with bull's eye maculopathy
options.C: Black bone spicule-shaped pigmentation in the peripheral retina
options.D: Drusen with haemorrhagic atrophic changes concentrated at the periphery of the retina
options.E: Pigmented choroidal neovascularisation throughout the retina

correct_answer_text: Black bone spicule-shaped pigmentation in the peripheral retina
explanation:
Retinitis pigmentosa Retinitis pigmentosa primarily affects the peripheral retina resulting in funnel vision

Features xnight blindness is often the initial sign xfunnel vision (the preferred term for tunnel vision) xfundoscopy: black bone spicule-shaped pigmentation in the peripheral retina, mottling of the retinal pigment epithelium

Associated diseases xRefsum disease: cerebellar ataxia, peripheral neuropathy, deafness, ichthyosis xUsher syndrome

xabetalipoproteinemia xLawrence-Moon-Biedl syndrome xKearns-Sayre syndrome xAlport's syndrome

subject: Ophthalmology
question: A 65-year-old man with a history of primary open-angle glaucoma presents with sudden painless loss of vision in his right eye. On examination of the right eye the optic disc is swollen with multiple flame-shaped and blot haemorrhages. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Central retinal vein occlusion - sudden painless loss of vision, severe retinal haemorrhages on fundoscopy

Sudden painless loss of vision

The most common causes of a sudden painless loss of vision are as follows: xischaemic optic neuropathy (e.g. temporal arteritis or atherosclerosis) xocclusion of central retinal vein xocclusion of central retinal artery xvitreous haemorrhage xretinal detachment

Ischaemic optic neuropathy xmay be due to arteritis (e.g. temporal arteritis) or atherosclerosis (e.g. hypertensive, diabetic older patient) xdue to occlusion of the short posterior ciliary arteries, causing damage to the optic nerve xaltitudinal field defects are seen

Central retinal vein occlusion xincidence increases with age, more common than arterial occlusion xcauses: glaucoma, polycythaemia, hypertension xsevere retinal haemorrhages are usually seen on fundoscopy

Central retinal artery occlusion xdue to thromboembolism (from atherosclerosis) or arteritis (e.g. temporal arteritis) xfeatures include afferent pupillary defect, 'cherry red' spot on a pale retina

Vitreous haemorrhage xcauses: diabetes, bleeding disorders xfeatures may include sudden visual loss, dark spots

Retinal detachment xfeatures of vitreous detachment, which may precede retinal detachment, include flashes of light or floaters (see below)

Differentiating posterior vitreous detachment, retinal detachment and vitreous haemorrhage

Posterior vitreous detachment Retinal detachment Vitreous haemorrhage

Flashes of light (photopsia) - in the peripheral field of vision Floaters, often on the temporal side of the central vision Dense shadow that starts peripherally progresses towards the central vision A veil or curtain over the field of vision Straight lines appear curved Central visual loss Large bleeds cause sudden visual loss Moderate bleeds may be described as numerous dark spots Small bleeds may cause floaters

subject: Ophthalmology
question: A 71-year-old man who has recently been diagnosed with macular degeneration asks for advice regarding antioxidant dietary supplements. Which one of the following may contraindicate the prescription of such supplements?
explanation:
Beta-carotene has been found to increase the risk of lung cancer and hence antioxidant dietary supplements arenot recommended for smokers. Age related macular degeneration

Age related macular degeneration is the most common cause of blindness in the UK. Degeneration of the central retina (macula) is the key feature with changes usually bilateral.

Traditionally two forms of macular degeneration are seen: xdry (geographic atrophy) macular degeneration: characterised by drusen - yellow round spots in Bruch's membrane xwet (exudative, neovascular) macular degeneration: characterised by choroidal neovascularisation. Leakage of serous fluid and blood can subsequently result in a rapid loss of vision. Carries worst prognosis

Recently there has been a move to a more updated classification: xearly age related macular degeneration (non-exudative, age related maculopathy): drusen and alterations to the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) xlate age related macular degeneration (neovascularisation, exudative)

Risk factors xage: most patients are over 60 years of age xsmoking xfamily history xmore common in Caucasians xhigh cumulative sunlight exposure xfemale sex

Features xreduced visual acuity: 'blurred', 'distorted' vision, central vision is affected first xcentral scotomas xfundoscopy: drusen, pigmentary changes

Investigation and diagnosis xoptical coherence tomography: provide cross sectional views of the macula xif neovascularisation is present fluorescein angiography is performed

General management xstop smoking xhigh dose of beta-carotene, vitamins C and E, and zinc may help to slow down visual loss for patients with established macular degeneration. Supplements should be avoided in smokers due to an increased risk of lung cancer

Dry macular degeneration - no current medical treatments

Wet macular degeneration xphotocoagulation xphotodynamic therapy xanti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) treatments: intravitreal ranibizumab
